name: Sensō-ji Temple

accessibility.notes: Main hall is reached by stairs; ramp and elevator available near the side entrance.

dress_notes: Shoulders covered is respectful at the main hall; no strict requirement outside.
best_time_notes: Arrive before 08:00 or after 18:00 to beat crowds. Kaminarimon lantern is lit at night.
summary: Tokyo's oldest Buddhist temple (founded 645) with the iconic Kaminarimon gate and the buzzing Nakamise shopping street leading to it.
description: Sensō-ji is dedicated to Kannon, the Bodhisattva of compassion. The giant red paper lantern at Kaminarimon gate is a Tokyo icon. Nakamise-dōri, the 250m approach, has been selling pilgrim snacks and souvenirs for centuries — try ningyō-yaki (doll-shaped sponge cakes). The temple grounds are free and open 24/7; the main hall is lit until 23:00.

name: Meiji Jingū

accessibility.notes: Gravel paths; main approach is flat and accessible.

dress_notes: No photography inside the inner hall during services. Respectful attire appreciated.
best_time_notes: Early morning for quiet forest paths. Watch for Shinto weddings on weekends (outer courtyard).
summary: Tokyo's grandest Shinto shrine, set in a hand-planted 70-hectare forest next to Harajuku Station.
description: Dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken, the shrine opened in 1920. Stroll the forested approach through massive torii gates — many donated sake barrels (kazaridaru) line the path. The adjacent Gyoen inner garden (¥500) has a photogenic iris pond in June.

name: Tokyo Skytree
best_time_notes: Clear winter mornings give the best Mt. Fuji sightings. Tembo Galleria sunset slots sell out first.
summary: At 634 m, the world's tallest free-standing tower, with two observation decks and on clear days a view of Mt. Fuji.
description: Opened in 2012 to replace Tokyo Tower as the city's broadcasting mast. The Tembo Deck (350 m) is the standard stop; Tembo Galleria (450 m) is an extra, spiralling glass ramp. Book online for a timed slot that skips the ticket queue entirely. The base has a large shopping complex (Solamachi) and an aquarium.

name: Shibuya Scramble Crossing

accessibility.notes: Crossing itself is flat with tactile paving.

best_time_notes: Most dramatic at night or during rain (umbrellas everywhere). Best photo spot: 2F Starbucks, or Shibuya Sky at dusk.
summary: The world's busiest pedestrian crossing — up to 3,000 people step off the curb on a single green light.
description: Stand outside Shibuya Station's Hachikō exit and watch the choreography, then cross yourself. For the bird's-eye shot, head up to Starbucks on the second floor of Tsutaya (free if you buy a drink) or book Shibuya Sky on top of Shibuya Scramble Square for a paid 360° view.

name: teamLab Planets Tokyo

accessibility.notes: Some rooms require walking through water; wheelchair and stroller access is limited. Contact venue for alternate route.

dress_notes: Avoid long flowing skirts or trousers you cannot roll up — you will walk barefoot through ankle-deep water in one room.
best_time_notes: Book the earliest or last slot for thinner crowds. Weekday afternoons are calmer.
summary: A barefoot journey through seven digital-art rooms — koi pools, mirrored orchids, boundaryless water landscapes.
description: The sister venue to teamLab Borderless, and easier to visit for first-timers. You leave your shoes at the entrance and wade through a shallow water room where koi swim around your legs via projection. Timed-entry tickets are mandatory and sell out days ahead in peak season.

name: Tsukiji Outer Market

accessibility.notes: Flat streets but narrow stalls and crowds make stroller navigation tough.

dress_notes: Closed-toe shoes recommended — wet stalls, scooter traffic.
best_time_notes: Go 07:00-10:00 for the freshest stalls. Closed most Sundays/Wednesdays — check the calendar.
summary: The lively retail side of the old fish market — grilled scallops, tamagoyaki skewers, sushi counters, knife shops.
description: The inner wholesale market moved to Toyosu in 2018, but the outer retail market remains — about 400 stalls selling seafood, produce, knives, tea, and ready-to-eat snacks. Hit Sushi Dai (queue-worthy), grab a tamagoyaki skewer from Marutake, then coffee at Turret Coffee. Most stalls take cash only.

name: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden

accessibility.notes: Paved paths; wheelchairs can be rented free at the entrance.

dress_notes: Alcohol and sports equipment are prohibited.
best_time_notes: Late March-early April for cherry blossoms; mid-November for autumn colours. Arrive at opening to avoid cherry-blossom crowds.
summary: A 58-hectare former imperial garden mixing French, English, and Japanese styles right next to Shinjuku Station.
description: Three distinct landscaped sections and a glass tropical greenhouse. In peak sakura, it hosts around 1,000 cherry trees of more than a dozen varieties, which stretches the bloom window considerably. Time-entry tickets can be booked online to skip the queue on peak weekends.

name: Ghibli Museum

accessibility.notes: Strollers must be checked at the entrance; wheelchair route available.

dress_notes: Indoor photography is prohibited; phones must be put away inside the galleries.
best_time_notes: Tickets open on the 10th of the preceding month at 10:00 JST on Lawson's Loppi. They sell out within hours, especially summer and weekends.
summary: Studio Ghibli's whimsical museum designed by Hayao Miyazaki himself — a must-book-ahead pilgrimage for animation fans.
description: A strictly timed-entry, photography-free museum that feels like a ride through Ghibli's imagination. Expect an exclusive short film (rotates monthly), hand-drawn animation rigs, a giant Laputa robot on the rooftop, and a winding staircase themed around Catbus. Ticketing is notoriously tricky — Lawson Loppi in Japan, or JTB abroad.

name: Tokyo National Museum

accessibility.notes: All six galleries wheelchair-accessible with elevators; audio guide supports multiple languages.

dress_notes: No flash. Some special exhibitions are photo-free — watch for signage.
best_time_notes: Open Tue-Sun; closed Mon (or Tue if Mon is a holiday). Weekday mornings are calmest.
summary: Japan's oldest and largest museum, with unrivalled collections of samurai armour, Buddhist sculpture, tea ceremony objects, and ukiyo-e prints.
description: Six buildings in Ueno Park, each with a different focus. Start with the Honkan (Japanese Gallery) for a greatest-hits run, then cross to the Heiseikan for archaeology, and the Tōyōkan for wider Asian art. Free under-18 entry; general admission covers the permanent collection — special exhibitions are separately priced.

name: Mt. Takao

accessibility.notes: Cable car lower station is accessible; the hiking trails are not suited to wheelchairs or strollers.

dress_notes: Wear trail shoes; Trail 1 is paved but others are dirt with stairs. Bring water.
best_time_notes: Late November for peak foliage. Sunrise summit climbs in summer are rewarded with a rare Tokyo view of Mt. Fuji.
summary: A 599 m forested mountain on the western edge of Tokyo with eight marked trails, a cable car, and soba stalls at the summit.
description: Trail 1 is paved and climbable in around 90 minutes; Trail 6 follows a stream and climbs past a small waterfall. Combine with the cable car or chair lift for a shorter family-friendly outing. Yakuō-in Temple en route is worth a stop.

name: Akihabara Electric Town

accessibility.notes: Sidewalks are flat; stores vary — many multi-story arcades have elevators but some retro-game shops are stairs-only.

dress_notes: Maid cafés and some shops restrict in-store photography — ask first.
best_time_notes: Main street (Chuo-dori) is pedestrianised Sundays 13:00-18:00 (April-September) and 13:00-17:00 the rest of the year.
summary: Neon-lit district for anime, manga, retro games, and hobby electronics — eight stories of vending-machine curiosities and claw machines.
description: Base your visit around Chuo-dori and its side streets. Super Potato (retro games), Mandarake Complex (used manga / figures), Yodobashi-Akiba (mega-electronics store), and the countless 'gachapon' capsule-toy floors are the greatest-hits stops. Stop at a themed café if you are curious, but stick to reputable ones — some entrance-fee scams exist.

name: Odaiba Waterfront

accessibility.notes: Mostly flat waterfront promenades; Yurikamome trains are level-boarding.

best_time_notes: Sunset over Rainbow Bridge is the headline. The driverless Yurikamome from Shimbashi is itself a ride.
summary: A man-made island in Tokyo Bay with the Rainbow Bridge view, a giant Gundam statue, shopping malls, and onsen/sento options.
description: A relaxed half-day for families or a sunset evening for couples. DiverCity Tokyo Plaza has the life-size Unicorn Gundam statue (free), Odaiba Beach is the photo spot for Rainbow Bridge, and Palette Town's giant Ferris wheel has been replaced by new developments — check current openings before you go.
